rows.prompt: At what peak data rate (in MT/s or GT/s) does the i.MX 93 support LPDDR4?
rows.rubric: Answer this knowledge-base question: 'At what peak data rate (in MT/s or GT/s) does the i.MX 93 support LPDDR4?'. Reference facts (may be incomplete or stale — verify against the SOURCE CONTEXT): ['3733', 'MT/s']. CORRECT = accurate answer, every claim grounded; ABSTAINED = says the sources don't cover it, or a partial-but-accurate answer; WRONG = fabricated or contradicted facts.
rows.raw: The i.MX 93 supports LPDDR4 at a maximum of 2880 MT/s in nominal drive mode, with low drive mode at 1866 MT/s and overdrive mode at 3733 MT/s. The datasheet notes that for the 9 x 9 mm package, the maximum data rate of LPDDR4x/LPDDR4 is 3200 MT/s.

rows.raw: The i.MX 93 has 6 Arm Cortex-A55 cores, while the i.MX 95 has up to 6 Arm Cortex-A55 cores. The datasheet lists the i.MX 95 with 6x Arm Cortex-A55, up to 1.8 GHz frequency.

Functional description 60.3.1 Controller mode The LPI2C controller logic operates independently from the target logic to perform all controller-mode transfers on the I2C bus. 60.3.1.1 Transmit and Command FIFO commands The transmit FIFO stores command data to initiate various I2C operations. The following operations can be initiated through commands in the transmit FIFO: • Start or repeated Start condition with address byte, expecting ACK or NACK. • Transmit data. This operation is the default for zero-extended-byte writes to the transmit FIFO. • Receive 1-256 bytes of data. You can configure this operation to discard received data and not to store it in the receive FIFO. • Stop condition. You can configure this operation to send a Stop condition when the transmit FIFO is empty. Multiple transmit and receive commands can be inserted between the Start and Stop conditions. To comply with the I2C specification, transmit and receive commands must not be interleaved. The receive data command and the receive data and discard commands can be interleaved. This interleaving ensures that only the desired received data is stored in the receive FIFO (or compared with the data match logic). The LPI2C controller automatically transmits a NACK on the last byte of a receive data command.

Table 588. LPI2C triggers Trigger Description Controller output trigger Generates an output trigger that can be connected to other peripherals on the device. The controller output trigger asserts on either a repeated Start or a Stop condition. The trigger remains asserted for one cycle of the LPI2C functional clock divided by MCFGR1[PRESCALE]. Target output trigger Generates an output trigger that can be connected to other peripherals on the device. The target output trigger asserts on either a repeated Start or a Stop condition that occurs after a target address match. The target output trigger remains asserted until the next target SCL pin negation. Input trigger Controls the start of a LPI2C bus transfer. The input trigger is synchronized. LPI2C clocks Clock Description LPI2C functional clock The LPI2C functional clock is asynchronous to the bus clock. It can remain enabled in low-power modes to support I2C bus transfers by the LPI2C controller. The functional clock is also used by the LPI2C target to support digital filter and data hold time configurations. The LPI2C controller divides the functional clock by a prescaler (MCFGR1[PRESCALE]) and the resulting frequency must be at least eight times faster than the I2C bus bandwidth. External clock The LPI2C target logic is clocked directly from the external pins. These pins are SCL and SDA, or SCLS and SDAS if the controller and target are implemented on separate pins). This clocking allows the LPI2C target to remain operational, even when the LPI2C functional clock is disabled. If the LPI2C functional clock is disabled, the LPI2C target digital filter must be disabled. The following operations can be initiated through commands in the transmit FIFO: • Start or repeated Start condition with address byte, expecting ACK or NACK. • Transmit data. This operation is the default for zero-extended-byte writes to the transmit FIFO. • Receive 1-256 bytes of data. You can configure this operation to discard received data and not to store it in the receive FIFO. • Stop condition. You can configure this operation to send a Stop condition when the transmit FIFO is empty. Multiple transmit and receive commands can be inserted between the Start and Stop conditions. To comply with the I2C specification, transmit and receive commands must not be interleaved. The receive data command and the receive data and discard commands can be interleaved. This interleaving ensures that only the desired received data is stored in the receive FIFO (or compared with the data match logic). The LPI2C controller automatically transmits a NACK on the last byte of a receive data command.

claims: The i.MX 93 has two Cortex-A55 cores in the Cortex-A55 MPCore platform, which operate up to 1.7 GHz.
It also has one Cortex-M33 core, which operates up to 250 MHz.
The NPU is a Neural Processing Unit (NPU) with neural network performance of 256 MACs operating up to 1.0 GHz and 2 OPS/MAC.
The NPU targets 8-bit and 16-bit integer RNN and handles 8-bit weights.

It supports the following features: • 256 MACs operating at up to 1.0GHz and 2 OPS/MAC • 2x 128-bit AXI master interfaces • 32-bit APB slave interface — The 128-bit M0 port is used by the NPU to access OCRAM. — The 128-bit M1 port is used by the NPU to access DRAM. • Q-channel slave port for interaction with the CCM and GPC clock and power control. 11.1.4 GIC-600 GIC-600 is used as the interrupt controller for the Cortex®-A55 processor. It supports a distributed microarchitecture containing several individual blocks that are used to provide a flexible GIC implementation. • Forward compatibility with ARMv8.2 Cores supporting increased 512 CPU threads/chip and multi-chip capabilities — Distributed architecture for reduced power, congestion and improved latency — End-to-End credited protocols allows bridging communication to any free-flowing transport layer. Transport layer will be native AXI4 stream. — Clock and power control for each block for improved power savings • QoS improvements — Increased ITS caching to reduce memory accesses — More flexible use of LPI cache and Pending Tables for reduced memory accesses and improved latency bounding • Improved trace and debug — PMU with full snapshot functionality — Full ITS command error logging and reporting via ARMv8.2 RAS error records — ECC error logging and containment to allow software recovery • Improved control over 1-of-N interrupt routing • SPI collators enabling Q-Channel support on main GIC 11.1.5 TrustZone The TrustZone architecture provides means to help secure systems, using the TrustZone Security Extensions, and Secure peripherals. TrustZone is a security feature on ARM Cortex M and A series that enables execution separation of trusted (secure) software, and enables access control isolation of trusted resources from non-trusted (non-secure) software and resources, while running on the same CPU. Memory arrays and peripherals are segmented into either Secure (S) or Non-Secure (NS). TrustZone is optimized for energy-efficient, embedded applications that require real-time responsiveness. More details on TrustZone can be found in “TrustZone® technology can be found at arm.com.

[1] FACT SHEET i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY i.MX 93 applications processors deliver efficient machine learning (ML) acceleration, energy flex architecture and state-of-the-art security to support energy-efficient edge computing. i.MX 93 processors offer fast and efficient ML inferencing along with a rich set of peripherals and high-performance application cores for automotive, industrial and consumer IoT market segments. TARGET APPLICATIONS • Automotive: domain controller compute off-load engine, driver monitoring system, audio, speech recognition, cost-effective gateway • Industrial Automation: gateways, remote I/O controllers, industrial scanners, HMI, machine vision • Building Control and Energy: energy meters, EV charging • Smart Home: home security hub, smart doorbell, smart lock, smart thermostat, AV receivers • Smart City: smart lighting, safety and security, traffic control PERFORMANCE COMPUTE ENGINE The i.MX 93 applications processors are the first in the i.MX portfolio to integrate the scalable Arm® Cortex®-A55 core, bringing best-in-class performance and energy efficiency to Linux-based edge applications. Based on Arm’s DynamIQ technology, the A55 core features the latest Armv8-A architecture extensions with dedicated instructions to accelerate machine learning (ML). NEURAL PROCESSING UNIT (NPU) The i.MX 93 family marks the industry’s first implementation of the Arm® Ethos™-U65 microNPU. A dedicated neural processing unit (NPU), Ethos-U65 delivers a combination of performance and efficiency with an optimized footprint that enables developers to create high-performance, cost- effective and energy-efficient ML applications. BUILT-IN MCU A 250 MHz Arm® Cortex®-M33 processor performs time- critical real-time compute and control. It can eliminate the need for an external microcontroller in the system design. The integrated Cortex-M33 core associated with the CAN FD interfaces provides a robust local control network for industrial applications. Additionally, the built-in Arm Cortex M33 in conjunction with the NPU can be used for low-power wake-word detection. i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY  [url] 2 CAMERA INTERFACES AND IMAGE PROCESSING The i.MX 93 family contains MIPI-CSI and parallel image sensor interfaces along with the NPU to support both monochrome and RGB (color) vision applications. The application processor offers a 2-lane MIPI-CSI camera interface capable of supporting 1080-p60 resolution and enables direct connection to external camera module and ISP. The application processors offer capabilities including down scaling, color space conversion, de-interlacing, alpha insertion, cropping and rotation of images for machine vision and other ML-related applications. DISPLAY AND MULTIMEDIA The i.MX 93 applications processors contain a 4-lane MIPI-DSI capable of supporting 1080p60 resolution, a 4-lane LVDS and parallel display interfaces capable of 720p60 resolution. Additionally, it features a high-efficiency pixel pipeline to perform 2D graphics processing to realize cost-effective GUI solutions. It is capable of image rotation (90°, 180°, 270°), image resize, color space conversion, multiple pixel format support (RGB, YUV444, YUV422, YUV420, YUV400) and standard 2D-DMA operations. SYSTEM SECURITY The i.MX 93 family implements security via NXP’s EdgeLock® secure enclave, a preconfigured, self-managed and autonomous security subsystem.

The i.MX 93 processor uses the Cortex A55 core with clock speeds up to 1.7 GHz. The Cortex-A55 processor core uses DynamIQ technology (the successor to Arm‘s big.LITTLE concept) and features the latest enhancements to the ARMv8.2-A architecture with a dedicated instruc­ tion set to accelerate machine learning (ML) models. According to NXP, the i.MX 93 processor is the first in the industry to implement ARM‘s Ethos-U65 microNPU with a performance of 256 MACs/cycle. The Ethos-U65 offers a very good combination of performance and efficiency in a very small size, enabling developers to realize high- performance, low-cost and energy-efficient ML applications. The i.MX 93 processor also contains a 250 MHz Cortex-M33 processor core for time-critical real-time computation and control and the EdgeLock Secure Enclave for providing the security functions. The memory interface is 16-bit wide and supports LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X with internal ECC support. In addition to up to 7 x I²S audio interfaces and 8-channel PDM microphone inputs, the processor offers extensive interfaces: CAN-FD, UARTs, SPI, QSPI, I²C and SDIO. Extensive security functions are also implemented. With the i.MX 93 processor, NXP offers a price- and feature-optimized CPU from the i.MX 9 series. Next to the i.MX 91 processor, the i.MX 93 processor is the smallest CPU in the i.MX 9 series and a good alternative to the i.MX 28 processor, i.MX 6UL/i.MX 6ULL processor for new designs. The main difference between this CPU and its pre­ decessors in terms of graphics and video interfaces is the addition of 24-bit RGB, MIPI-DSI and LVDS interfaces. A total of four CPU variants are available, from single-core to dual-core with/without NPU and qualified to operate at different temperature range The most important interfaces are available as follows: • 1x MIPI DSI 4 Lanes (display serial interface) • 1x LVDS 4 Lanes • 1x MIPI CSI 2 Lanes (camera sensor interface) • 3x SDIO supporting SD/eMMC/Wi-Fi • 2x USB 2.0 • 2x Gigabit Ethernet (1x TSN) • 2x CAN-FD • 8x UART, 8x I²C, 8x SPI, 7x I²S • 1x QSPI • 1x 4-ch, 12-bit ADC A serial camera interface (MIPI-CSI) allows a camera to be connected directly to the CPU and supports its use in digital imaging applications. The i.MX 93 processor is based on the same Arm Core architecture as the entire i.MX 9 series.

[1] FACT SHEET i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY i.MX 93 applications processors deliver efficient machine learning (ML) acceleration, energy flex architecture and state-of-the-art security to support energy-efficient edge computing. i.MX 93 processors offer fast and efficient ML inferencing along with a rich set of peripherals and high-performance application cores for automotive, industrial and consumer IoT market segments. TARGET APPLICATIONS • Automotive: domain controller compute off-load engine, driver monitoring system, audio, speech recognition, cost-effective gateway • Industrial Automation: gateways, remote I/O controllers, industrial scanners, HMI, machine vision • Building Control and Energy: energy meters, EV charging • Smart Home: home security hub, smart doorbell, smart lock, smart thermostat, AV receivers • Smart City: smart lighting, safety and security, traffic control PERFORMANCE COMPUTE ENGINE The i.MX 93 applications processors are the first in the i.MX portfolio to integrate the scalable Arm® Cortex®-A55 core, bringing best-in-class performance and energy efficiency to Linux-based edge applications. Based on Arm’s DynamIQ technology, the A55 core features the latest Armv8-A architecture extensions with dedicated instructions to accelerate machine learning (ML). NEURAL PROCESSING UNIT (NPU) The i.MX 93 family marks the industry’s first implementation of the Arm® Ethos™-U65 microNPU. A dedicated neural processing unit (NPU), Ethos-U65 delivers a combination of performance and efficiency with an optimized footprint that enables developers to create high-performance, cost- effective and energy-efficient ML applications. BUILT-IN MCU A 250 MHz Arm® Cortex®-M33 processor performs time- critical real-time compute and control. It can eliminate the need for an external microcontroller in the system design. The integrated Cortex-M33 core associated with the CAN FD interfaces provides a robust local control network for industrial applications. Additionally, the built-in Arm Cortex M33 in conjunction with the NPU can be used for low-power wake-word detection. i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY  [url] 2 CAMERA INTERFACES AND IMAGE PROCESSING The i.MX 93 family contains MIPI-CSI and parallel image sensor interfaces along with the NPU to support both monochrome and RGB (color) vision applications. The application processor offers a 2-lane MIPI-CSI camera interface capable of supporting 1080-p60 resolution and enables direct connection to external camera module and ISP. The application processors offer capabilities including down scaling, color space conversion, de-interlacing, alpha insertion, cropping and rotation of images for machine vision and other ML-related applications. DISPLAY AND MULTIMEDIA The i.MX 93 applications processors contain a 4-lane MIPI-DSI capable of supporting 1080p60 resolution, a 4-lane LVDS and parallel display interfaces capable of 720p60 resolution. Additionally, it features a high-efficiency pixel pipeline to perform 2D graphics processing to realize cost-effective GUI solutions. It is capable of image rotation (90°, 180°, 270°), image resize, color space conversion, multiple pixel format support (RGB, YUV444, YUV422, YUV420, YUV400) and standard 2D-DMA operations. SYSTEM SECURITY The i.MX 93 family implements security via NXP’s EdgeLock® secure enclave, a preconfigured, self-managed and autonomous security subsystem.

The i.MX 93 processor uses the Cortex A55 core with clock speeds up to 1.7 GHz. The Cortex-A55 processor core uses DynamIQ technology (the successor to Arm‘s big.LITTLE concept) and features the latest enhancements to the ARMv8.2-A architecture with a dedicated instruc­ tion set to accelerate machine learning (ML) models. According to NXP, the i.MX 93 processor is the first in the industry to implement ARM‘s Ethos-U65 microNPU with a performance of 256 MACs/cycle. The Ethos-U65 offers a very good combination of performance and efficiency in a very small size, enabling developers to realize high- performance, low-cost and energy-efficient ML applications. The i.MX 93 processor also contains a 250 MHz Cortex-M33 processor core for time-critical real-time computation and control and the EdgeLock Secure Enclave for providing the security functions. The memory interface is 16-bit wide and supports LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X with internal ECC support. In addition to up to 7 x I²S audio interfaces and 8-channel PDM microphone inputs, the processor offers extensive interfaces: CAN-FD, UARTs, SPI, QSPI, I²C and SDIO. Extensive security functions are also implemented. With the i.MX 93 processor, NXP offers a price- and feature-optimized CPU from the i.MX 9 series. Next to the i.MX 91 processor, the i.MX 93 processor is the smallest CPU in the i.MX 9 series and a good alternative to the i.MX 28 processor, i.MX 6UL/i.MX 6ULL processor for new designs. The main difference between this CPU and its pre­ decessors in terms of graphics and video interfaces is the addition of 24-bit RGB, MIPI-DSI and LVDS interfaces. A total of four CPU variants are available, from single-core to dual-core with/without NPU and qualified to operate at different temperature range The most important interfaces are available as follows: • 1x MIPI DSI 4 Lanes (display serial interface) • 1x LVDS 4 Lanes • 1x MIPI CSI 2 Lanes (camera sensor interface) • 3x SDIO supporting SD/eMMC/Wi-Fi • 2x USB 2.0 • 2x Gigabit Ethernet (1x TSN) • 2x CAN-FD • 8x UART, 8x I²C, 8x SPI, 7x I²S • 1x QSPI • 1x 4-ch, 12-bit ADC A serial camera interface (MIPI-CSI) allows a camera to be connected directly to the CPU and supports its use in digital imaging applications. The i.MX 93 processor is based on the same Arm Core architecture as the entire i.MX 9 series.

[4] PLATFORM OPTIONS

The i.MX 93 applications processors family, part of the 
EdgeVerse™ portfolio platform, offers multiple SoCs with 
a scalable option to move up or down depending on the 
application needs. The different products in the i.MX 93 
family include capabilities such as an integrated NPU and 
the number of Cortex-A55 cores. Additionally, pin-to-pin 
compatibility is planned between i.MX 93 and future i.MX 9 
series product families.

rows.prompt: Write a clear, friendly email to a colleague introducing the NXP i.MX 95 for a new edge-AI product. Cover what it is, its Neutron NPU, and why it suits edge inference. Ground the specifics in the datasheets.
rows.raw:
Subject: NXP i.MX 95: a good fit for edge inference

Hi [Colleague's name],

We're evaluating processors for our next edge-AI product, and the i.MX 95 is worth a look. Here's the key information:

**What it is**
- i.MX 95 applications processors are the first i.MX devices to support functional safety with a built-in Arm Cortex-M33, which can be configured as a safety island.
- They offer up to six Arm Cortex-A55 cores at up to 1.8 GHz, plus a Cortex-M7 and a Cortex-M33. The A55s share a 512 kB TCM, and the M7 and M33 get 16 kB cache each.
- Memory is one x32 LPDDR interface at up to 6400 MT/s in LPDDR5 mode or 4266 MT/s in LPDDR4X mode. They also have 3x uSDHC, 8x LPI2C and 8x LPSPI, plus 2x I3C and an Octal SPI.
- The i.MX 95 IEIEC data sheet covers the Industrial product.

**The Neutron NPU**

Field Function 23-16 RDTERM Read Terminate Counter Determines when to terminate a read operation: • For I2C, this field controls when to NACK a read. • For I3C, this field can be used to terminate (end) a read: — If RDTERM is 0, it has no effect. — If RDTERM is 1, the read terminates after the next character. — If RDTERM is 2, the read terminates after the next two characters. The field supports up to 255 characters. In DDR mode, RDTERM terminates the read based on word counts (for DDR) instead of byte counts (for SDR). The field self-clears when MSTATUS[COMPLETE] becomes 1. You may write 1 to this field anytime, but a value greater than 1 must be written when starting EmitStartAddress. Completion of a manual IBI means that the target DA is known, and so the mandatory byte (or not) is specified by the application when acknowledging. This field is also used when a message is emitted in Message mode using the MWMSG_SDR or MWMSG_DDR registers. If an IBI with MDB (mandatory byte) is ACKed, the controller limits it to a maximum of eight more bytes after the MDB. RDTERM = 1 can be used with REQUEST = NONE to terminate data from a target sooner. If this field is 0b, it indicates ACK (acknowledge). When REQUEST = 1 (EmitStartAddr) or REQUEST = 7 (AutoIBI), Controller In-band Interrupt Registry and Rules (MIBIRULES) decides whether to ACK with mandatory byte. When REQUEST = 3 (IBIAckNack), ACK with no mandatory byte. If this field is 1b, it indicates NACK (reject) or no acknowledgement. If this field is 10b, it indicates acknowledge with mandatory byte. rows.prompt: Write a clear, friendly email to a colleague introducing the NXP i.MX 95 for a new edge-AI product. Cover what it is, its Neutron NPU, and why it suits edge inference. Ground the specifics in the datasheets.
rows.raw:
Hi [Colleague's Name],

Excited to share the i.MX 95 for our edge-AI product. It's the first i.MX with Arm Cortex-A55 cores and the Ethos-U65 microNPU, plus the Energy Flex architecture for industrial/IoT/automotive.

**CPU and NPU at a glance**
- Up to 6 Arm Cortex-A55 cores at up to 1.8 GHz, 32 kB L1 cache per core, 64 kB L2 cache per core and a shared 512 kB L3, all fully 64-bit capable.
- The Ethos-U65 microNPU provides efficient machine-learning inference, working with the CPU to deliver higher performance and lower power.
- Memory: one x32 LPDDR interface at up to 6400 MT/s in LPDDR5 mode or 4266 MT/s in LPDDR4X mode.

**Neutron NPU specifics**
- Four eIQ® Neutron N3-1024S NPUs per part.
- 1492 kB total TCM, with 512 kB of TCM for the instruction and data combined.
- The NPU architecture diagram shows weight decoder, rescaler/shifter, activation engine, and data canvas buffers, with its own DMA.
- The reference manual gives the NPU an optimized path for MAC compute blocks, weight management, memory access, rescaling, activation, and pooling.
- It boots from any core downloading the firmware library into the NPU's built-in RISC-V core ITCM. The CPU then requests execution, and the NPU reads model and input data from addresses the CPU specifies.

**Why it suits edge inference**
- **Low power.** The reference manual says the NPU is the first in the industry to implement the Ethos-U65 microNPU with 256 MACs/cycle, and the CPU-NPU combination is said to deliver higher performance and lower power than the CPU alone.
- **Self-contained inference.** The NPU can access system memory and fetch its own program code, data, and parameters while it runs. It generates interrupts or messages when an operation completes, and you can query it through a mailbox.
- **Rich set of peripherals.** Industrial-grade packages, including 3x uSDHC, 8x LPI2C and 8x LPSPI, plus eMMC5.1.
- **Security and safety.** Industrial and extended industrial qualification, and the Cortex-M33 as a safety island.

**Datasheet notes**
- The i.MX 95 data sheet lists the Cortex-A55 features in the feature summary, and the reference manual provides the NPU's block diagram, operator summary, and detailed register-level information.

rows.prompt: Write a clear, friendly email to a colleague introducing the NXP i.MX 95 for a new edge-AI product. Cover what it is, its Neutron NPU, and why it suits edge inference. Ground the specifics in the datasheets.
rows.raw:
Subject: New edge-AI product: i.MX 95 with Neutron NPU

Hi [Colleague's Name],

I'm excited to introduce the i.MX 95 with Neutron NPU for our new edge-AI product. Here's the key info from the datasheet:

**i.MX 95 at a glance**
- Up to 6 Arm Cortex-A55 cores at up to 1.8 GHz, plus 1x Cortex-M7 at up to 800 MHz and 1x Cortex-M33 at up to 333 MHz.
- 19 x 19 mm package with one x32 LPDDR interface at up to 6400 MT/s in LPDDR5 mode or 4266 MT/s in LPDDR4X mode. Smaller 15 x 15 mm package at 4266 MT/s in LPDDR5 mode or 4000 MT/s in LPDDR4X mode.
- 3x uSDHC (SD3.0, SDIO3.0, eMMC5.1), 8x LPI2C, 8x LPSPI, 2x I3C, 1x Octal SPI.
- Industrial, extended industrial, commercial and automotive level qualification, backed by NXP's product longevity program.

**Neutron NPU**
- A dedicated machine-learning accelerator that works with the CPU to raise performance and lower power for neural network inference.
- On-chip hardware with an architecture that processes Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) compute blocks, rescales, shifts, provides activation functions and pooling, and manages memory accesses.
- The NPU is booted by any core that downloads the firmware library into the NPU's ITCM. Once started, the CPU can then request it to execute models and read results from system memory.
- The NPU supports a subset of TFLite operators, including ABS, ADD, AVERAGE_POOL_2D, CONV_2D, DEPTHWISE_CONV_2D, ELU, EXP, FULLY_CONNECTED, HARD_SWISH, and more.
- The reference manual gives a block diagram showing the architecture, with compute pipelines, buffers, and a data canvas that enables data reuse.

**Why it suits edge inference**
- **Small, efficient CPU**: The Cortex-A55 cores are optimized for energy efficiency, so the NPU can run inference with minimal host CPU involvement.
- **Autonomous NPU**: It can access system memory, fetch its own code, and read model and input data from addresses the CPU specifies, then write results back.
- **TFLite-compatible operators**: You can import trained and quantized NNs into eIQ Toolkit, which generates an NPU-optimized model.
- **Flexible memory and scale**: With 512 kB TCM and

rows.prompt: Using the datasheets, what does the i.MX 95 Neutron NPU do, and what are its key features?
rows.raw:
The Neutron N3-1024S NPU in the i.MX 95 is an on-chip hardware accelerator that provides efficient processing of machine-learning workloads, working in conjunction with the CPU to deliver higher performance and lower power consumption for neural-network inference. Its key features, per the i.MX 95 reference manual:

- 1024 MACs operating at up to 1.0 GHz and 2 OPS/MAC, with 2.0 TOP/s performance.
- Natively supports convolutional neural networks (CNN), including Atrous Separable Convolution and Depthwise Separable Convolutional networks, with matrix sizes of 1x1, 3x3, 5x5, and 7x7, plus stride and padding support.
- Supports Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), including minimum gated unit (MGU) networks.
- Supports activation function, including ReLu, PreLu, and LeakyReLu.
- Supports sampling or reshaping functions and element-wise operations.
- Supports layer operations

rows.prompt: Using the datasheets, generate a concise one-page product brief for the NXP i.MX 95: overview, NPU, memory/connectivity, and target markets.
rows.raw:
**NXP i.MX 95 Overview**
- A multi-domain, multi-core design with Cortex-A55, Cortex-M7, and Cortex-M33 cores
- On-chip eIQ® Neutron N3-1024S NPU for efficient machine-learning inference, plus 1 MB SRAM (1024 MACs at up to 1.0 GHz)
- Supports LPDDR5/LPDDR4X (Inline ECC & Encryption) and has 1492 kB OCRAM (ECC)
- Includes a Mali™ 3D GPU, 2x MIPI-CSI 4-lane (1 mux w/DSI) and 1x MIPI-DSI 4-lane (w/PHY)
- Connectivity: 2x 1 GbE (w/TSN), 2x PCIe® Gen 3.0 x12, 10 GbE (w/TSN), 3x SD/SDIO3.0 / eMMC5.1, and more
- The eIQ® Neutron N3-1024S NPU is listed in the i.MX 95 Data Sheet for Industrial Products (IMX95IEC) as a feature, and the i.MX 95 Reference Manual describes it in its NPU Domain Overview.

**NPU (eIQ® Neutron N3-1024S)**
- 1024 MACs operating at up to 1.0 GHz, with 2 OPS/MAC
- Natively supports CNN, RNN, and activation functions such as ReLu, PreLu, LeakyReLu
- Provides rescaling, activation, and pooling functions, and supports normalization functions and element-wise operations
- 1 MB local SRAM

**Memory and Connectivity**
- LPDDR5/LPDDR4X (Inline ECC & Encryption)
- 1492 kB OCRAM (ECC)
- 2x 1 GbE (w/TSN), 2x PCIe® Gen 3.0 x12, 10 GbE (w/TSN)
- 3x SD/SDIO3.0 / eMMC5.1, Octal SPI FLASH (inline crypto)
- Includes a Mali™ 3D GPU and 2x MIPI-CSI 4-lane (1 mux w/DSI) plus 1x MIPI-DSI 4-lane (w/PHY)

**Target Markets**
- Industrial and IoT applications, where the datasheet lists as market drivers: reducing energy consumption, lowering resource usage and waste, and the rise of ransomware, IoT as a target, intelligent edge, Industry 4.0, and machine learning proliferation.

NOTE 11.3 SMMU-700 This chip supports ARM System-level Memory Management Unit (SMMU) SMMU-700 for memory management and conversion of virtual input address to physical output address. This translation is based on address mapping and memory attribute information that is available from configuration tables and translation tables that are stored in memory. SMMU can support up to two stages of translation: • One TCU in NoC domain • Three TBUs in Wakeup domain • One DTI interconnect (DTI_IC0) in Wakeup domain • Eight TBUs in NoC domain • One DTI interconnect (DTI_IC1) in NoC domain • Two AXI-4 Stream SSIs for the DTI interface between Wakeup domain: DTI_IC0 and NoC domain DTI_IC1 • SMMU performs translation table walks for each stage of translation and supports up to 48 bit VA (virtual address). • SMMU TTB1 table must be disabled using EPD1 (disable) fields in the Context Descriptor for the existence of TTB1 table. There is no sharing of the Cortex-A MMU tables and IO-SMMU translation tables. SMMU Bypass There are cases where the traffic must logically bypass the TBU.

Block diagram 107.1.2 Features Below is a list of features supported on iEP-RC: • Presents as a PCIe Root Complex that contains Event Collectors, and integrates with Integrated End Point (RCiEP or iEP) - For easy software discovery of peripheral functions and error reporting; leverage the infrastructure built into OSes and RTOS for PCIe. • Discoverable capabilities at a granular level - Software can discover what features/capabilities exists; allow an easy upgrade path. • 7'd2 ECAM buses to provide access to the PCIe Config space of the iEP and RCEC • 7'd2 Root Complex Event Collectors (RCEC) • Generate PCIe wired interrupt to the system on receiving error or Power Management Event message from iEP 107.1.3 PCI/PCIe Background It is useful to have an understanding of PCI/PCIe to be able to understand PCI Root Complex Integrated Endpoints. This section is intended to give an overview for those not familiar with PCI, not to provide a detailed explanation. 107.1.3.1 Overview PCI and its successor PCI Express (PCIe) provide a framework for connecting peripheral devices to a computer consisting of one or more CPU(s) and memory. PCI defines how such devices are discovered and integrated into the system. This includes: • Assignment of addresses for registers and memory in the device, determining how the "host system" accesses these • Assignment, configuration, and control of interrupts including various types of message signaled interrupts (MSI) • Reporting and handling certain errors • Handling power management including events that will cause the system to exit low power modes • Adding and removing such devices to a “live” system (hotplug) NXP Semiconductors Integrated Endpoint Root Complex (iEP-RC) i.MX 95 Applications Processor Reference Manual, Rev. 5, 2026-03-30 Reference Manual 6381 / 11263  PCI is defined for a multi-connect, parallel bus and PCIe for a serial interconnect. Devices can be arranged into a tree topology through the use of bridges or switches. Both PCI and PCIe are intended to be used with pluggable cards and are often used with peripherals on the same circuit board. None the less the use of PCI with peripheral devices which are integrated into an SoC is becoming common as it allows using the extensive standardized approaches and software infrastructure created for PCI with these integrated peripherals simplifying software development and portability across different SoCs. With PCI, system software (boot firmware, OS, …) is initially only aware of a PCI controller -- a device which acts as the bridge between the host and the PCI/PCIe. It is not aware of any devices connected to this controller.

rows.prompt: Using the datasheets, generate a concise one-page product brief for the NXP i.MX 95: overview, NPU, memory/connectivity, and target markets.
rows.raw:
**NXP i.MX 95 Overview**
- Dual-core Arm Cortex-A55 CPU at up to 1.7 GHz with the latest Cortex-A55 enhancements for machine learning (ML) and the Ethos-U65 microNPU.
- Low power, small size, and a wide temperature range (-40 to 125°C).
- Long product life (minimum 10 or 15 years) and industrial certifications.
- Security features include TrustZone, secure boot, firmware update authentication, and EdgeLock secure subsystem.
- Extensive crypto services, run-time attestation, and a silicon root of trust.

**NPU**
- ARM Ethos-U65 microNPU with 256 MACs/cycle.
- Supports LIN 1.3, LIN 2.0, LIN 2.1, and SAE J2602/1 with a LIN controller layer.
- Optional eSCI DMA support on two instances.

**Memory and Connectivity**
- 16-bit memory interface supporting LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X with internal ECC.
- On-chip memory includes 2MB flash and 512kB SRAM.
- Interfaces: MIPI DSI, LVDS, UARTs, SPI, QSPI, I²C, SDIO.
- PCIe 2.0 integrated as the iEP-RC.

**Target Markets**
- Industrial, where long lifecycles and extreme operating conditions matter (temperature, cold start, junction temperature).
- Edge computing, streaming media, rich 2D & 3D graphics, advanced audio and voice processing, touch sensing, vision.
- Systems where security, low power, and fine-grained power partitioning are key.

NXP Semiconductors Ethernet and Network Controller (NETC) i.MX 95 Applications Processor Reference Manual, Rev. 5, 2026-03-30 Reference Manual 5285 / 11263  106.3.4.2.2.1 Entry Elements Entry elements store data needed by hardware and/or software to implement the required functionality. The following three types of entry elements are supported: • Key Elements - a key element contains the key data, which is used to identify an entry in a table. Typical key data components are fields found in a frame and used to perform table lookups during frame processing, for example, MAC address, VLAN ID, and so on. Other key data components may be used to locate the key element in a table or to identify a table instance to use, for example, entry precedence or hardware resource identifier. Two types of Key Element exist within the NTMP protocol: — Exact Match Key Element: used within the context of exact match tables. This key element can be used to perform any operation. When querying the Exact Match Key Element, the queried result will match exactly the data which was supplied when performing the add operation on the entry. — Ternary Match Key Element: used in the context of ternary match tables. Generally, this type of Key Element is composed of three pieces of information–a precedence, data and a data mask. The precedence portion of the Key Element will be used to determine the matching entry in the event that several entries' data/mask combinations match a lookup. This key element can be used to perform the add operation only. The precise data stored in the hardware will be compressed based on the mask portion of the Key Element. Thus, when querying the Ternary Match Key Element, the queried result will not match precisely the value of the Key Element which was supplied when adding the entry. When querying, the precedence portion of the key and the data mask portion of the key will always be returned as it was set by an add or update operation. The data portion, however, will be returned as an expansion of the masked data stored in the hardware; that is any bit in the data whose corresponding data mask bit was a "don't care" (matching to either a ‘0’ or ‘1’) will return as '0' when querying, regardless of the state of this bit in the original data portion of the key. • Configuration Elements - a configuration element contains data that originates from the software control plane. The data stored in the configuration elements is used by the hardware to implement the required datapath processing. • Status Elements - a status element contains data that typically originates from the hardware. The data stored in the status elements is used by the hardware to inform the software about the state of its resources. Software can read status elements from the hardware and in some cases software can update the element, however, hardware can change the value of the element at any time.

NOTE 11.3 SMMU-700 This chip supports ARM System-level Memory Management Unit (SMMU) SMMU-700 for memory management and conversion of virtual input address to physical output address. This translation is based on address mapping and memory attribute information that is available from configuration tables and translation tables that are stored in memory. SMMU can support up to two stages of translation: • One TCU in NoC domain • Three TBUs in Wakeup domain • One DTI interconnect (DTI_IC0) in Wakeup domain • Eight TBUs in NoC domain • One DTI interconnect (DTI_IC1) in NoC domain • Two AXI-4 Stream SSIs for the DTI interface between Wakeup domain: DTI_IC0 and NoC domain DTI_IC1 • SMMU performs translation table walks for each stage of translation and supports up to 48 bit VA (virtual address). • SMMU TTB1 table must be disabled using EPD1 (disable) fields in the Context Descriptor for the existence of TTB1 table. Block diagram 107.1.2 Features Below is a list of features supported on iEP-RC: • Presents as a PCIe Root Complex that contains Event Collectors, and integrates with Integrated End Point (RCiEP or iEP) - For easy software discovery of peripheral functions and error reporting; leverage the infrastructure built into OSes and RTOS for PCIe. • Discoverable capabilities at a granular level - Software can discover what features/capabilities exists; allow an easy upgrade path. • 7'd2 ECAM buses to provide access to the PCIe Config space of the iEP and RCEC • 7'd2 Root Complex Event Collectors (RCEC) • Generate PCIe wired interrupt to the system on receiving error or Power Management Event message from iEP 107.1.3 PCI/PCIe Background It is useful to have an understanding of PCI/PCIe to be able to understand PCI Root Complex Integrated Endpoints. This section is intended to give an overview for those not familiar with PCI, not to provide a detailed explanation. 107.1.3.1 Overview PCI and its successor PCI Express (PCIe) provide a framework for connecting peripheral devices to a computer consisting of one or more CPU(s) and memory. PCI defines how such devices are discovered and integrated into the system. This includes: • Assignment of addresses for registers and memory in the device, determining how the "host system" accesses these • Assignment, configuration, and control of interrupts including various types of message signaled interrupts (MSI) • Reporting and handling certain errors • Handling power management including events that will cause the system to exit low power modes • Adding and removing such devices to a “live” system (hotplug) NXP Semiconductors Integrated Endpoint Root Complex (iEP-RC) i.MX 95 Applications Processor Reference Manual, Rev. 5, 2026-03-30 Reference Manual 6381 / 11263  PCI is defined for a multi-connect, parallel bus and PCIe for a serial interconnect. Devices can be arranged into a tree topology through the use of bridges or switches. Both PCI and PCIe are intended to be used with pluggable cards and are often used with peripherals on the same circuit board. None the less the use of PCI with peripheral devices which are integrated into an SoC is becoming common as it allows using the extensive standardized approaches and software infrastructure created for PCI with these integrated peripherals simplifying software development and portability across different SoCs. With PCI, system software (boot firmware, OS, …) is initially only aware of a PCI controller -- a device which acts as the bridge between the host and the PCI/PCIe. It is not aware of any devices connected to this controller.

rows.raw:
**NXP i.MX 95 Overview**
- 32-bit Arm Cortex-A55 CPU at up to 1.7 GHz, with NEON and FPU
- 4K Video Processing Unit and Image Signal Processor
- eIQ Neutron N3-1024S NPU for efficient machine-learning workloads
- Secure Enclave for device-wide security intelligence, run-time attestation, and key management
- Pin and software-architecture compatibility with previous i.MX 8 and 9 generations for maximum platform reuse
- Extensive security features, including a silicon root of trust, anti-tamper silicon, and security provisions in eFuses and OTP

**NPU: eIQ Neutron N3-1024S**
- 4x Neutron compute pipelines with 256 MACs/cycle
- Provides efficient processing of machine-learning workloads in conjunction with the main CPU
- Features: weight decoder, rescaler/shifter, activation engine, data canvas, and control

**Memory & Connectivity**
- Memory: LPDDR5/LPDDR4X (x32), with inline ECC and encryption
- NPU domain: 1 MB SRAM (TCM) available to the system when not in use by the NPU
- Connectivity: 2x 1 GbE with TSN, 2x PCIe Gen 3.0 x12, 10 GbE with TSN, 2x MIPI-CSI (4-lane with DSI), 1x MIPI-DSI (4-lane with PHY), SPDIF Tx/Rx, 2x 32-bit FlexIO ADC (8-channel, 12-bit), 3x SD/eMMC5.1, 2x 32-bit FlexIO ADC, 8-ch PDM mic input, 2-lane I2S TDM Tx/Rx, 4x CAN-FD, 6x UART/USART, 6x I2C, 6x SPI

**Target Markets**
- Industrial: machine vision, factory automation, energy, and building automation
- IoT: smart cameras, security systems, and smart sensors
- Consumer: smart home, wearables, and portable devices
